1.pericope_label: I am the Lord your God: after the doings of Egypt and Canaan shall ye not do

schools.summary: Gill reports from Diodorus that Egyptian law, against the custom of all others, allowed men to marry their own sisters. Calvin says the eastern nations never scrupled at incestuous marriages, a brother having no abhorrence of marrying his uterine sister nor an uncle his niece, and were so dead to shame as to trample on all the laws of nature — which is why God here enumerates the kinds of incest, whose mention would else have been superfluous. On the promise of life Calvin will have nothing but the higher sense: eternal life is promised to all who keep the Law, and those who expound the passage of this transitory life are mistaken. Scripture denies justification by works, he adds, not because the Law is imperfect but because our corruption makes the promise of none effect: the defect arises from the infirmity of men, not the doctrine of the Law. And salvation is not to be had from it unless every precept is complied with.

Henry says that after divers ceremonial institutions God returns to moral precepts, the former still of use to us as types and the latter still binding as laws, and unfolds the title: the Lord, who has a right to rule all; your God, who has a peculiar right to rule you, and to whom you are accountable. He sees something to be unlearned, which they had sucked in with their milk in Egypt: it would be the greatest absurdity to keep such affection for their house of bondage as to be governed in their devotions by its usages; yet they were in danger of inheriting the vices of Canaan along with its land. Such a tyrant is custom, Henry says, that their practices are called ordinances, and became rivals with God's own. On the promise he grants that it still stands, with a favourable construction of the condition, so that if we keep the commandments in sincerity, though we come short of sinless perfection, the way of duty is the way of comfort; but not as a covenant under which the least transgression excludes us for ever. The alteration the gospel has made is in the last word: still the man that does them shall live, but not live in them, for the law could not give life, being weak through the flesh and not in itself.

Clarke takes the doings to include the worship of demons and beasts named earlier, and the abominations that follow here. Wesley explains the repetition of the divine title: the things forbidden here were practised and allowed by the gentiles, to whose custom God opposes his own authority; and he says the two nations are named because living among them made their example the more dangerous, though all other nations are included under them. On the promise Wesley puts it as covenant against covenant: by the covenant of works none since the fall could be justified, obedience needing to be perpetual; by the covenant of grace this life is promised to all who obey sincerely.

Ellicott marks the turn, since unlike the communications just before, which treated of ritual and ceremonial pollutions, the enactments Moses is here told to deliver touch the moral life — precepts forming the basis of domestic purity and the foundation of human happiness. He makes the warning run against past and future at once, and notes that even the acts that were legalised are condemned, as having no authority. On the promise he would render it live by or through them, and takes it of a happy and prosperous life, since disobedience exposed the offender to death; but he notes that the second Temple authorities read it of eternal life, the Chaldee versions rendering it shall have life eternal. Keil notes that the words I am Jehovah your God stand at the head and are repeated at the close, enforcing observance as a covenant obligation and urging it by the promise of life.

6.pericope_label: None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin, to uncover their nakedness

schools.summary: Gill notes the double reach of the command from the plural verb, which cautions male and female alike, and reports that the Talmudists took the doubled noun to comprehend Gentiles as well as Israelites. Calvin takes the phrase the other way from Wesley, holding that not only are incestuous connections out of wedlock condemned, but the degrees are marked within which marriage itself is unlawful. He faces the objection that the Law being abrogated these obligations are dissolved, and answers that what is prescribed here is not merely political but deduced from the source of rectitude itself, and from natural feelings implanted in us; what is natural cannot be abrogated by consent or custom, and the barbarism that prevailed in the East does not nullify the chastity opposed to it.

Henry takes the phrase chiefly to forbid the marrying of these relations, but adds that uncleanness committed with any of them outside marriage is no less intended, and with it everything that has the appearance of the evil. He gives the reasons behind the rule, and thinks them reasonable quite apart from the authority that enacts them. By marriage two were to become one flesh; those already in a sense one flesh by nature could not therefore, without the greatest absurdity, become one flesh by institution, the institution being designed to unite those not united before. And marriage puts an equality between husband and wife, so that where inequality is founded in nature, as between parents and children or uncles and nieces, it cannot without confusion be taken away by the equality of marriage. Brothers and sisters he treats as the one case where equals are forbidden, granting there is no such natural absurdity in it, since Adam's sons must have married their own sisters; but positive law was requisite, for if every man married his own sister each family would be a world to itself, and it would be forgotten that we are members one of another.

Wesley stands alone against the rest, thinking it highly probable, on Mr Free's showing, that the phrase does not mean marriage but fornication throughout this chapter. Clarke reasons from social consequence: intermarriage with other families strengthens and extends the bonds of compact, so that love of neighbour becomes a practicable duty, and feuds and wars are prevented.

Ellicott reads the opening literally as man, man, the idiom used earlier in the book, and renders it no man whatsoever; he draws an inference from what is missing, since the words of the house of Israel, which elsewhere complete the phrase, are absent here, showing that these prohibitions bind the resident stranger too, lest the land be defiled by his transgressions. He states the central question plainly: on the import of uncovering nakedness depends whether these interdicts refer to illicit commerce or to incestuous marriages. In the one other place in the Pentateuch where it occurs it implies nothing unseemly, and some high authorities therefore maintain that here it denotes extra-conjugal licentiousness only; but comparing what follows, Ellicott concludes it is used of intercourse both within and without matrimony, since among the early Hebrews cohabitation without any ceremony constituted marriage. Keil explains that flesh of his flesh means a flesh belonging to the same flesh as himself, and so a blood-relation, and agrees that the prohibition relates to both married and unmarried intercourse, though chiefly to the former.

7.pericope_label: The nakedness of thy father, thy mother, thy sister, thy father's wife

schools.summary: Gill grants that it was once necessary for a man to marry his sister, since there was no one else for the first family to marry, but says that when mankind had increased the thing became unlawful; the Egyptians kept it up in imitation of Isis and Osiris, the Persians following Cambyses. On the father's wife he states the reach of the ban from the other end, that it held after the father's death, though she had only been betrothed, and even though the father had divorced her.

Ellicott notes that the received rendering of the first prohibition rests on the interpretation current in the second Temple, by which it is addressed to daughter and son alike, so that the Chaldee of Jonathan gives it as the woman shall not lie with her father, and the man shall not lie with his mother — the case contemplated being that of Lot's daughters. The clause may however be read straight through, on the ground that the two being one flesh, the shame of the one is the shame of the other. He gives the second Temple's working definition of the next law: a father's wife is for ever prohibited, whether betrothed or married, divorced or not, widowed or not; and a man who lies with her while her husband lives is doubly guilty, first because she is near of kin and secondly because she is another man's wife. By that rule Ellicott sorts the biblical instances: Reuben with Bilhah and Absalom with his father's wives were adultery rather than incestuous marriage, their husbands being alive and the wives undivorced, whereas the sin at Corinth lay in sons actually marrying their divorced stepmothers while their fathers lived. On the sister he finds the old excuse working in Israel, since Adam wedded bone of his bone and his sons their own sisters, and Abraham himself married a half-sister; explicit as the law is, the story of Amnon and Tamar shows the practice continuing in spite of it. Keil explains why a step-mother falls under the same ban: she stood in blood-relationship only to the son whose mother she was, but for the father's sake she was inaccessible, and the offence was capital. He restricts the sister-clause to the half-sister, taking born at home or born abroad not of legitimacy but of a first marriage, and notes that the word used of such commerce elsewhere, which commonly means sparing love or favour, here means dishonour and shame.

debates.question: Why does the law appear to forbid the same half-sister twice?

there is no repetition: the earlier verse treats the son by a second marriage, this one the son by a first

12.pericope_label: Thy father's sister, thy mother's sister, thy daughter in law, thy brother's wife

schools.summary: Gill notes that Maimonides forbade the aunt whether she stood in lawful wedlock or not, and reports a reading of the uncle clause that takes it of sodomy, before preferring the plainer sense, that the following words explain the phrase. Calvin will have nothing to do with the levirate exception, and calls those bad interpreters who raise a controversy on the passage; it is incongruous, he says, to twist into different senses declarations made in the same place and the same words, so that if it is unlawful to marry the wife of a father or a son or an uncle, the same must hold of a brother's wife, enacted in the very same context. He knows where the mistake began: the levirate command has been ignorantly restricted to own-brothers, whereas it is a well-known Hebrew idiom to embrace all near kinsmen under that name, and it was on that footing that Boaz married Ruth. Were own-brothers really included, he argues, then on the same grounds a father-in-law must marry his daughter-in-law and a son-in-law his mother-in-law, which it is an abomination to speak of. As for Er and Onan, both married to Tamar, he answers that Judah followed the received practice of the Gentiles and acted improperly in permitting it.

Clarke and Wesley both read the last of these prohibitions as bounded by the levirate: the ban refers only to cases where the deceased brother left children, for if he died childless the survivor not only might but was required to marry the widow.

Keil gives the ground of the prohibitions in a word: an aunt on either side is barred because she is the blood-relation of the father or mother, and the wife of a father's brother because through her the uncle himself was dishonoured. He notices that the penalty attached to these in the parallel chapter is not death at the magistrate's hand but that the persons shall bear their iniquity, and in the last case shall die childless — from which he concludes that the offence was to be punished by God himself rather than by the court. On the daughter-in-law he marks the word used of that offence elsewhere, which comes from a root meaning to mix, and denotes a sinful confounding of the divine ordinances — used in only one other connection, of a woman lying with a beast. Ellicott adds that the law current in the time of Christ extended the ban even to half-sisters born to the grandfather out of wedlock; and he observes what is remarkable in the lawgiver's own case, since Moses was the offspring of such an alliance, his father Amram having married Jochebed, his own father's sister. On the aunt by the mother's side he records a striking asymmetry: the second Temple authorities understood the prohibition strictly of nephew and aunt, but not conversely of niece and uncle; the latter they reckoned an especially meritorious act. On the brother's wife Ellicott presses the consequence — since the law elsewhere enjoins that marriage as a moral and civil duty, and heaps public indignity on the brother-in-law who refuses it, the prohibition here cannot rest on the ground of incest at all, for what is inherently incestuous the divine law would never have set aside.

17.pericope_label: Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sister, to vex her, in her life time

schools.summary: Gill records a rabbinic disagreement about the woman and her daughter: Jarchi held that a man who did not marry the woman but only defiled her was free to marry her daughter, whereas Aben Ezra held that if he had lain with the mother the daughter was forbidden. Calvin comes at the sister-clause from the other side, against those who infer from the words in her lifetime that a widower may marry his wife's sister. They ought to have considered the legislator's intention from his express words, since mention is made not only of filthiness but of the jealousy and quarrels that arise from it; the licence for polygamy is here restricted by an exception, that the Israelites should be contented with one evil and not set two sisters at hostile contention. The first wife's condition was painful enough in having a rival, worse in constant quarrelling with her near relation. Hence Calvin does not restrict the name of sister to actual sisters, but includes other relations whose marriages would not otherwise be incestuous; it is not incest that is condemned here, he says, so much as the cruelty of a husband. He ends with a caution: since long custom has established that cousins-german do not marry, we must beware of giving scandal, remembering Paul's admonition to abstain even from lawful things when they are not expedient.

Clarke says the prohibition is of two sisters at the same time, as Jacob had Rachel and Leah, and finds nothing in the law to make it illegal to marry a sister-in-law once her sister is dead, since the text says in her lifetime; though he adds that some think the words may be understood to forbid polygamy as well. Wesley reads it round the other way, suggesting that what is forbidden is perhaps not simply taking one wife to another, but doing it in such a manner or for such an end that a man may vex or revenge himself upon the first.

Ellicott states the first case simply: a man who marries a widow with a daughter by a former husband is forbidden the daughter as well; and the second Temple's administrators held that if he married either and she died he could not afterwards marry the other, though the bar did not extend to illicit commerce. On the sister-clause he will not allow the reading that makes it forbid polygamy, and argues it down at length. The marginal rendering one wife to another, first proposed by Junius and Tremellius in the sixteenth century, is contrary to the words wife and sister, which throughout these prohibitions invariably mean just that; and where the like phrase is used metaphorically for one and another it always carries a distributive force, which is not the case here. It is besides at variance with a code that legislates throughout on the assumption of polygamy, forbidding a king to multiply wives — which, as Bishop Patrick remarks, is not a prohibition of more than one but of an excessive number — and framing a law of primogeniture that presupposes a man with two wives. And the Jews themselves have always read it of two sisters, as the Chaldee, the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac all do. Keil renders the difficult verb as packing the two together into one marriage bond, so placing the sisters in carnal union through their common husband and disturbing the sisterly relation — as the marriage forced upon Jacob had evidently done; he notes that no punishment is fixed, and that after the first wife's death a man was at liberty to marry her sister.

debates.question: Does this clause forbid marrying two sisters, or polygamy itself?

19.pericope_label: Thou shalt not approach unto a woman as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness

schools.summary: Gill draws the plain inference that not even a man's own wife was excepted, much less another woman.

Henry approaches the verse from the side of what it protects rather than what it forbids, calling it a law to preserve the honour of the marriage bed — that it should not be unseasonably used, and, in the verse following, that it should not be invaded by an adulterer. He then gathers the arguments by which the whole section is enforced, observing that he who has an indisputable right to command us yet condescends to reason with us, drawing with the cords of a man. First, sinners defile themselves with these abominations: all sin is defiling to the conscience, but these have a peculiar turpitude in them, and our heavenly Father in kindness requires that we keep ourselves clean and do not wallow in the dirt. Second, the souls that commit them shall be cut off — and justly, for if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy. Third, the land itself is defiled, made unfit to have God's tabernacle in it, rendered unwholesome to the inhabitants, and loathsome to all good men in it, as the wickedness of Sodom was to the soul of righteous Lot. Fourth, these had been the practices of the former inhabitants, so that the laws were necessary as antidotes are necessary when men go into an infected place. Henry turns that last argument into a rule of self-examination: when we observe how ill sin looks in others, we should use the sight as an argument with ourselves to keep our own purity with the utmost care.

Clarke sends the reader back to the earlier law of separation for the details. Wesley alone asks what becomes of the law under the gospel, and answers that it stands: this was not only a ceremonial pollution but an immorality besides, which is why the prophet places it among gross sins in a list of moral offences, and therefore it is unlawful still.

Ellicott marks a change of subject at this verse, since the marriage laws are done and what follows treats of sexual impurities, suggested to some extent by the matters that had to be discussed in regulating the alliances just prohibited. He distinguishes the penalties, since a man who consorted with her without knowing her condition contracted defilement for seven days, whereas both parties who did it presumptuously were visited with death; and he notes that Ezekiel reckons the breach of this law among the heinous sins of Israel. Keil explains the term as covering the uncleanness of a woman's hemorrhage, whether the monthly flow or that which follows childbirth, called elsewhere the fountain of bleeding, and reads the penalty in the parallel chapter as the cutting off of both from their people, that is, death.

outliers.note: Argues that this law is not merely ceremonial but moral, and therefore still binding under the gospel, since the prophet lists its breach among gross sins.

themes: thou shalt not approach unto a woman as long as she is put apart
the honour of the marriage bed
the arguments by which these laws are enforced

20.pericope_label: Thou shalt not let any of thy seed pass through the fire to Molech

schools.summary: Gill files adultery under the seventh commandment, and notes that the sin named at the close of these verses takes its common name from the inhabitants of Sodom, for whose sake that city was destroyed by fire. Calvin explains why adultery is set apart from simple fornication: all fornication pollutes a man, but there is grosser impurity in adultery, because the sanctity of marriage is violated and a spurious offspring derived. On the closing declaration he takes it as an appeal to the first commandment, God claiming the worship due to him alone, with an implied contrast to all fictitious idols — since I am the eternal God, and have chosen you as my peculiar people, I would have you separated from all defilements.

Clarke sets out three opinions about what passing through the fire meant — that what was offered was the human seed, that the children were made a burnt offering outright, or that they were not burnt at all but passed between two fires by way of consecration — and will not decide flatly between the last two. Several scriptures, he grants, seem strongly to intimate that some were burnt alive; but the rabbins assert the milder rite, and he presses a case in point: Ahaz is said to have made his son pass through the fire, and yet Hezekiah succeeded him on the throne, so that there it can only have been a consecration, his idolatrous father meaning to initiate him early in the service of the demon. Wesley allows both, that it was done either by burning them in the fire or by making them pass between two great fires, which was a kind of consecration to that god; and he notes that this idol belonged chiefly to the Ammonites and answers to the Saturn of the heathen, named here because Israel's neighbours were most infected with it, though under the one instance every other kind of idolatry is comprehended.

Ellicott finds the order deliberate, since those who violate the sanctity of the marriage tie will readily sacrifice their children, so that the prohibition of offering them follows naturally on the laws of unchastity. He preserves the traditional description of the idol — a temple outside Jerusalem with seven compartments, entered according to the gift, the seventh reserved for him who offered his son; the image was kissed, a fire kindled within until the arms glowed, and drums beaten to drown the child's cries, lest the father hear and be moved with pity. He explains the profaning of the name as consisting in this, that other nations would say the Israelites reckoned their own God an inferior deity, since to him they offered animals while to Molech they gave their children. On adultery he notes that the penalty fell alike on the betrothed and the married woman, and sets beside it what other nations did: in Egypt the adulterer received a thousand strokes and the woman had her nose cut off. Keil identifies the idol as an old Canaanitish deity, called by the Phoenicians and Carthaginians Melkarth, related to Baal, a sun-god worshipped, like Kronos and Saturn, by the sacrifice of children; it was a hollow brazen statue that could be heated, bull-headed, with arms stretched out to receive what was given, and from the time of Ahaz children were slain in the valley of Ben-hinnom and laid in those heated arms. On the last prohibition he observes that it forbids the sin of Sodom, to which the heathen were more or less addicted and from which even the Israelites did not keep themselves free.

23.pericope_label: Defile not ye yourselves: the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbinic extension of the prohibition to any beast whatever, small or great, tame or wild, fowls being comprehended as well. Calvin explains why such things had to be named at all: an old proverb says that good laws have sprung from evil habits, and these monstrosities would have been buried in eternal silence had not necessity compelled God to bring them to light; but the Canaanites had advanced to such a pitch that sins which else would have stayed hidden were familiarly known among them. From the same fact he draws a second point, that in saying these abominations prevailed among the Gentiles God indicates that evil habits are no excuse at all, and that public consent is vainly alleged in defence of vice. Calvin closes by contrasting the Law with the abominations just named: that the Gentiles, being destitute of light, should be drawn aside in every direction was not surprising, but it behoved true believers on the contrary to testify that they were not children of darkness but of light.

Clarke says such practice was often done in Egypt, on the testimony of Herodotus, and observes that the offence is punishable with death by the laws of his own country too. On the great figure of the passage he calls it a very nervous personification, in which the land is an intelligent being with a deep and refined sense of moral good and evil: word of the abominations of the people is brought to it, and it is so affected that a nausea is produced and it vomits out its own inhabitants. It was natural for the inspired penman to use such a figure, Clarke adds, since the description he was obliged to give must have affected him nearly as he represents the land to be affected. Wesley notices who is bound by the statutes: the stranger as well as the Israelite, of whatever nation or religion; for though they might not force such a man to submit to their religion, they might restrain him from public contempt of their laws and from violating natural law, which besides the offence against God was a matter of evil example to the Israelites themselves.

Ellicott thinks the necessity of the prohibition appears the more when it is remembered that the practice actually formed part of the religious worship of the Egyptians in connection with their goat deities. He notes the symmetry of the chapter's close: the Lawgiver who introduced these precepts with five verses of preamble now concludes with an equally solemn appeal to observe them in their integrity, since the violation of them has branded those nations with infamy and brought about their destruction and expulsion from the very land which is now to be given to Israel. On the figure of the land he builds the doctrine further: from the creation the earth has shared in the punishment of man's guilt, and at the restitution of all things she is to share in his restoration, so that her physical condition hangs upon his moral conduct — when he disobeys she is parched and withholds her fruit, when he keeps the commandments she is blessed. Keil marks the term the text applies to the last offence, the same word used earlier of the daughter-in-law, meaning a confusion or mixing up of what God had distinguished; and he observes that the verbs about the land are prophetic perfects and the language poetical, the land being personified as a living creature which violently rejects food that it dislikes.

27.pericope_label: That the land spue not you out also: therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance

schools.summary: Gill sums up the indictment against the former occupants: the men of the land who dwelt in Canaan before Israel came into it were guilty of unclean copulations and incestuous marriages, of fornication and adultery, of bestiality and of idolatry. He draws the warning back to the beginning of things, that by sinning upon it they rendered the land obnoxious to the curse of God, as the whole earth originally was for the sin of man, so that they might expect to be cast out of Canaan as Adam was cast out of paradise.

Wesley says the phrase of cutting off must be understood variously, either of ecclesiastical or of civil punishment, according to the differing natures of the offences for which it is inflicted. Clarke closes on the practical use: the only way to be preserved from all false worship is seriously to consider and devoutly to observe the ordinances of the true religion, and he who in the things of God goes no farther than he can say, Thus it is written, and thus it behoves me to do, is never likely to receive a false creed or to perform a superstitious act of worship. From that he turns to the law itself with something like wonder. How true is that word, that the law of the Lord is perfect: in a small compass, and in a most minute detail, it comprises everything calculated to instruct, direct, convince, correct and fortify the mind of man; whatever has a tendency to corrupt or injure him, that it forbids, and whatever is calculated to comfort him and secure his best interests, that it commands. Since the human soul is polluted and tends to pollution, Clarke adds, the great doctrine of the law is holiness to the Lord. He ends by setting the two gifts side by side: magnify God for his law, for by it is the knowledge of sin, and magnify him for his gospel, for by this is the cure of sin.

Ellicott presses a point of translation at the warning. The verb here is the same one used a few verses earlier of the land vomiting out its inhabitants, and by rendering it vomit in the one place and spue in the other the Authorised Version needlessly weakens the striking connection between the two. He takes the sentence against the offender to particularise every individual, so that anyone whatever, male or female, who is guilty will incur the punishment prescribed; and he reads the cutting off as meaning that where the transgression escapes the notice of the tribunal, God himself will inflict the penalty — a necessary distinction, since some of the crimes named in this chapter are elsewhere to be visited with death by the hand of man. He finds one more word mistranslated at the close, and thinks the loss considerable: what the Authorised Version calls abominable customs are properly abominable statutes, since these things were not practised merely as usages but were legally enacted as the statutes of the land and formed part of the religious institutions of those nations, which is exactly the point made at the opening of the chapter. He notes too that the declaration with which the group of laws began is the declaration with which it ends, and that the repetition imparts a peculiar solemnity to the whole.

themes: that the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it
the souls that commit them shall be cut off from among their people
therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance: I am the Lord your God
